newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Stark plays down hopes of big EMU group.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Stark plays down hopes of big EMU group.

text.p: Juergen Stark, number two at Germany's Finance Ministry, played down expectations on Tuesday that the single European currency launch would go ahead with a big starting lineup.
Although some would-be members may meet the criteria set by the Maastricht Treaty, Stark said many were not yet ready.
"There are members whose economic structures are not yet well-enough prepared to take part in (European monetary union)," Stark told a conference of German newspaper editors.
"Certainly, there are member states that qualify on paper," Stark said.

"But in practice they would be well-advised to maintain exchange flexibility for a certain period, and... respect that they should not have to follow the rigid rules of the European Central Bank from the start."

Stark, who is regarded as Chancellor Helmut Kohl's man in the Finance Ministry and is seen as a hard-liner on monetary union, said countries should forsake the political prestige they might win from joining economic and monetary union (EMU) at the planned start in 1999.
He did not name any names, but his comments appeared directed at countries like Italy or Spain, which have not yet established a track record of exchange rate stability.

"For me, the markets have overdone expectations that a large number of countries can qualify," Stark said. "We have to make sure that these countries also stand for stability. Only then, does this project have a lasting chance of success."
He added the calm within the European exchange rate mechanism was an indication that financial markets were betting on a broad-based EMU.

"There are certain expectations in the market that a large number of European countries are going to start. There is calm in the exchange rate mechanism. It's being speculated that this is already a foregone conclusion," he said.
"I believe that there can be no foregone conclusions. The point of no return is in 1998," Stark added.
The 1997 economic performance of European Union member states will be reviewed early next year to decide which countries are eligible to join EMU.
Stark gave no direct comment on whether he expected EMU to go ahead on schedule, but said "fundamentally, stability still comes before the timetable."
